---
title: "Visualizations"
---
```{python}
#| include: false
import os
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer, ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS
import numpy as np

master_df = pd.read_csv("data/processed/master.csv")
decade_order = ["1980s", "1990s", "2000s", "2010s", "2020s"]
master_df["lyric_word_count"] = master_df["lyrics"].dropna().apply(lambda x: len(str(x).split()))
master_df["genre"] = master_df["seed_query"].str.extract(r"^(\w+(?:\s\w+)?)\s+year:")
```

## Lyric Word Count by Decade

```{python}
#| label: wordcount-by-decade
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Lyric word count distribution by decade"

import plotly.express as px

decade_order = ["1980s", "1990s", "2000s", "2010s", "2020s"]

plot_df = master_df.dropna(subset=["lyric_word_count"]).copy()
plot_df = plot_df[plot_df["lyric_word_count"] >= 0]

fig = px.violin(
    plot_df,
    x="decade",
    y="lyric_word_count",
    category_orders={"decade": decade_order},
    color="decade",
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Set2,
    box=True,   # closest equivalent to showing distribution summary
    points=False,
    labels={
        "decade": "Decade",
        "lyric_word_count": "Word Count",
    },
    height=500,
)

fig.update_traces(
    meanline_visible=False,
    spanmode="hard"
)

fig.update_layout(
    title="Lyric Word Count Distribution by Decade",
    showlegend=False,
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=50, b=0),
)

fig.update_yaxes(
    title="Word Count",
    range=[0, 2000],
    showgrid=True,
    gridcolor="lightgray"
)

fig.update_xaxes(title="Decade")

fig.show()
```

There is a clear and consistent decline in lyric word count from 1980s to 2020s. 

When zooming out, we can see that the 1980s and 1990s distributions are wide and tall, with substantial mass in the upper range indicating that long-form lyrics were common in those decades. The 1990s in particular shows the widest spread, likely reflecting the dominance of hip hop and RnB in that era which, as seen in the genre analysis, tend toward higher word counts. From the 2000s onward the distributions become progressively narrower and more bottom-heavy. 

This decade-level word count signal is potentially useful as a feature for the classifier, though as noted in the genre analysis, it may partially reflect the shifting genre composition of each decade rather than a pure temporal trend in songwriting style.

## Word Count Over Time
```{python}
#| label: wordcount-time
#| fig-cap: "Mean and median lyric word count by release year."
#| echo: false

yearly = (
    master_df
    .dropna(subset=["lyric_word_count", "release_year"])
    .groupby("release_year")["lyric_word_count"]
    .agg(["mean", "median", "count"])
    .reset_index()
)
yearly = yearly[yearly["count"] >= 10]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=yearly["release_year"], y=yearly["mean"],
    name="Mean", line=dict(color="#6C4FBF", width=2)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=yearly["release_year"], y=yearly["median"],
    name="Median", line=dict(color="#D85A30", width=2, dash="dash")))
fig.update_layout(
    title="Lyric Word Count Over Time",
    height=420,
    xaxis_title="Release Year",
    yaxis_title="Word Count",
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=55, b=0),
    legend=dict(
        orientation="h",
        y=1.08,
        x=0,
    ),
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    showgrid=False,
    tickmode="linear",
    dtick=5
)

fig.update_yaxes(
    showgrid=True,
    gridcolor="lightgray",
    zeroline=False
)

fig.show()
```

The mean lyric word count is highly volatile across years, with notable spikes in the early 1980s and a dramatic peak around 1997–1998 that likely reflects the dominance of hip hop and rap in that era. The median, by contrast, remains far more stable throughout, hovering in the 300–500 word range across all decades. The persistent and wide gap between mean and median suggests that a small number of unusually long songs are pulling the average upward in most years, though this skew does appear to shrink from the 2000s onward as both lines converge


## Top TF-IDF Terms by Decade
```{python}
#| label: tfidf-interactive
#| fig-cap: "Top 15 lyrical terms per decade after stopword removal. Select a decade from the dropdown."
#| echo: false

LYRICS_STOPWORDS = set(ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS).union({
    "oh","yeah","ooh","ah","uh","na","la","hey","ha","woah","whoa","mmm","hm",
    "gonna","wanna","gotta","ain","don","didn","won","can't","couldn","isn",
    "know","like","just","got","get","let","come","go","say","said","want",
    "need","love","baby","time","way","day","night","life","heart","feel",
    "make","take","give","look","away","back","right","ll","ve","re","em",
    "cause","til","bout","chorus","verse","bridge","hook","repeat",
    "x2","x3","x4","lyrics","contributors","genius","embed","outro","intro",
    "translations","english","translation","spanish",
    "que","la","te","el","en","se","yo","da","le","si","mi","pa","tu","lo","es",
})

decade_docs = {
    d: " ".join(master_df.loc[master_df["decade"] == d, "lyrics"].dropna().tolist())
    for d in decade_order
}

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    max_features=5000,
    stop_words=list(LYRICS_STOPWORDS),
    min_df=2,
    ngram_range=(1, 2),
    token_pattern=r"(?u)\b[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z]+\b"   # removes numeric junk like 2018 / 10
)

tfidf_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(list(decade_docs.values()))
feature_names = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()

# better palette than pastel
colors = px.colors.qualitative.Set2

traces = []
buttons = []

for i, decade in enumerate(decade_order):
    scores = tfidf_matrix[i].toarray().flatten()
    top_idx = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:15]

    top_words = [feature_names[j] for j in top_idx][::-1]
    top_scores = [scores[j] for j in top_idx][::-1]

    traces.append(
        go.Bar(
            x=top_scores,
            y=top_words,
            orientation="h",
            marker=dict(color=colors[i % len(colors)]),
            name=decade,
            visible=(i == 0),
            hovertemplate="<b>%{y}</b><br>TF-IDF: %{x:.3f}<extra></extra>"
        )
    )

    visibility = [j == i for j in range(len(decade_order))]
    buttons.append(
        dict(
            label=decade,
            method="update",
            args=[
                {"visible": visibility},
                {"title": {"text": f"Top 15 TF-IDF Terms in the {decade}"}}
            ]
        )
    )

fig = go.Figure(data=traces)

fig.update_layout(
    title={"text": f"Top 15 TF-IDF Terms in the {decade_order[0]}", "x": 0.08},
    height=520,
    showlegend=False,
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=110, r=30, t=110, b=60),
    xaxis_title="TF-IDF Score",
    yaxis_title="",
    updatemenus=[
        dict(
            buttons=buttons,
            active=0,
            direction="down",
            x=0.5,
            y=1.22,
            xanchor="left",
            yanchor="top",
            pad={"r": 10, "t": 0},
            bgcolor="white",
            bordercolor="lightgray",
            borderwidth=1
        )
    ]
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    showgrid=True,
    gridcolor="lightgray",
    zeroline=False
)

fig.update_yaxes(
    showgrid=False,
    automargin=True
)

fig.show()
```

The TF-IDF terms reveal a clear evolution in lyrical vocabulary across decades. The 1980s are defined by rock and pop imaginery such as "man", "rock", "light", "dance", and "beat". The 1990s show a sharp shift toward hip hop wordplay, with explicit language and African-American Vernacular English terms alongside others like "man" and "girl". The 2000s mark the first appearance of Spanish-language tokens ("por," "est," "os," "para"), signaling the growing presence of Latin music in the corpus. This trend accelerates dramatically in the 2010s and especially the 2020s, where the top terms are almost entirely Spanish ("est," "qu," "por," "los," "pero," "una," "como"), reflecting Latin music's rise to mainstream dominance. 

Across all decades, a small set of English words such as "man", "girl", "good", "tell" persist, suggesting some universal lyrical anchors regardless of era or genre.


## Artist Country of Origin by Decade
```{python}
#| label: country-decade
#| fig-cap: "Top 8 artist countries per decade. Select decade from the dropdown."
#| echo: false

buttons = []
traces = []

for i, decade in enumerate(decade_order):
    subset = master_df[master_df["decade"] == decade]
    top_countries = subset["mb_country"].dropna().value_counts().head(8)
    visible = (i == 0)
    traces.append(go.Bar(
        x=top_countries.values[::-1],
        y=top_countries.index[::-1],
        orientation="h",
        marker_color=colors[i],
        name=decade,
        visible=visible,
    ))
    visibility = [j == i for j in range(len(decade_order))]
    buttons.append(
        dict(
            label=decade, 
            method="update",
            args=[
                {"visible": visibility},
                {"title": {"text": f"Top Artist Countries of Origin in the {decade}"}}
            ]
        )
    )

fig = go.Figure(data=traces)
fig.update_layout(
    title={"text": f"Top Artist Countries of Origin in the {decade_order[0]}", "x": 0.08},
    height=520,
    updatemenus=[
        dict(
            active=0, 
            buttons=buttons, 
            x=0.8, 
            y=1.11,
            xanchor="left", 
            yanchor="top", 
            pad={"r": 10, "t": 0},
            bgcolor="white",
            bordercolor="lightgray",
            borderwidth=1,
            direction="down")],
    xaxis_title="Number of artists",
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=60, b=0),
    showlegend=False,
)

fig.update_xaxes(
    showgrid=True,
    gridcolor="lightgray",
    zeroline=False
)

fig.update_yaxes(
    showgrid=False,
    automargin=True
)

fig.show()
```

The US dominates artist origin across all five decades. Beyond that, the composition shifts over time. 

The 1980s are defined by Anglophone and Western European representation: GB is nearly on par with the US, followed by IT, DE, CA, FR, and AU. The 1990s see GB drop sharply and Latin countries (MX, AR) and Turkey enter the picture for the first time. The 2000s cement Latin America's rise with MX and PR both cracking the top 4, while GB recovers slightly. The 2010s shift toward Northern Europe, with NL, SE, and NO appearing alongside GB and FR, suggesting the global spread of electronic and pop production. By the 2020s, the landscape is dramatically different, as PR jumps to second place and MX, CO also rank highly, reflecting Latin music's dominance, while South Korea (KR) enters the top 8, signaling K-pop's growing global footprint. GB, once nearly equal to the US in the 1980s, falls to seventh.

```{python}
#| label: pageviews-setup
#| include: false
pv_df = master_df[master_df["pageviews"].notna()].copy()
pv_df["log_pageviews"] = np.log10(pv_df["pageviews"])
```

## Page Views vs. Word Count
```{python}
#| label: pageviews-wordcount
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Pageviews vs lyric word count colored by decade. Longer lyrics do not necessarily drive higher engagement."

scatter_df = pv_df.dropna(subset=["lyric_word_count"]).copy()
scatter_df = scatter_df[scatter_df["lyric_word_count"] <= 6500] 

fig = px.scatter(
    scatter_df,
    x="lyric_word_count",
    y="log_pageviews",
    color="decade",
    category_orders={"decade": decade_order},
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Pastel,
    hover_data=["track_name", "artist_name", "pageviews"],
    opacity=0.5,
    trendline="lowess",
    trendline_scope="overall",
    trendline_color_override="#333333",
    labels={
        "lyric_word_count": "Lyric Word Count",
        "log_pageviews": "Pageviews (log₁₀)",
    },
    height=480,
)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=5))
fig.update_layout(
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=20, b=0),
    legend_title="Decade",
)
tickvals = [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=tickvals, ticktext=[f"10<sup>{v}</sup>" for v in tickvals])
fig.show()
```

The vast majority of songs cluster below 1000 words with very large variance and no clear correlation between word count and pageviews. The LOWESS trendline peaks around 1000-1200 words and declines steadily afterward, indicating that beyond a moderate length, longer lyrics are actually associated with lower engagement. Songs exceeding 2000 words are sparse and rarely achieve high pageviews.

Decade-wise, 2020s songs (green) dominate the low word-count end, consistent with the trend toward shorter lyrics, while older decades like the 1990s and 2000s extend further right. Overall, word count is a weak predictor of popularity.

## Sentiment by Decade
```{python}
#| label: sentiment-by-decade
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "VADER sentiment score by decade. Scores range from -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive). A decline toward negative sentiment in recent decades may reflect shifting lyrical themes."

fig = px.violin(
    master_df.dropna(subset=["sentiment"]),
    x="decade", y="sentiment",
    color="decade",
    category_orders={"decade": decade_order},
    color_discrete_sequence=colors,
    box=True,
    hover_data=["track_name", "artist_name"],
    labels={"sentiment": "VADER Sentiment Score", "decade": "Decade"},
    height=430,
)
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="gray", opacity=0.5,
              annotation_text="neutral", annotation_position="right")
fig.update_layout(
    showlegend=False,
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=20, b=0),

fig.show()
```

Sentiment distributions are broadly similar across all decades, with medians consistently in the positive range and full spreads reaching both extremes. However, a subtle but steady downward shift is visible from the 1980s onward. The 2010s and 2020s show the most balanced upper-lower split, suggesting lyrics have become more emotionally ambivalent over time. 

## Repetition Ratio by Decade
```{python}
#| label: repetition-by-decade
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Repetition ratio by decade, proportion of lines that are duplicates within a song."

fig = px.violin(
    master_df.dropna(subset=["repetition_ratio"]),
    x="decade", y="repetition_ratio",
    color="decade",
    category_orders={"decade": decade_order},
    color_discrete_sequence=colors,
    box=True,
    hover_data=["track_name", "artist_name"],
    labels={"repetition_ratio": "Repetition Ratio", "decade": "Decade"},
    height=430,
)
fig.update_layout(
    showlegend=False,
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=20, b=0),
)
fig.show()
```

Repetition ratio increases gradually and consistently from the 1980s to the 2010s, with medians rising and interquartile ranges shifting upward over time. The 1980s distribution is wide and bottom-heavy, with considerable mass near zero indicating many songs with low repetition, while the 1990s show a similar but slightly tighter spread. From the 2000s onward, the bulk of the distribution consolidates in the middle range, and by the 2010s the median reaches its highest point across all decades. The 2020s pull back slightly, with a lower median and a more compressed distribution, though still higher than the 1980s and 1990s baseline. This trend toward higher repetition may reflect the increasing dominance of pop and hip hop genres, which tend to rely more heavily on chorus-driven structures and catchy hooks, as well as broader shifts in songwriting style favoring simplicity and memorability.

## Rhyme Density by Decade
```{python}
#| label: rhyme-by-decade
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Rhyme density by decade, proportion of line endings that share a rhyme sound with another line."

fig = px.violin(
    master_df.dropna(subset=["rhyme_density"]),
    x="decade", y="rhyme_density",
    color="decade",
    category_orders={"decade": decade_order},
    color_discrete_sequence=colors,
    box=True,
    hover_data=["track_name", "artist_name"],
    labels={"rhyme_density": "Rhyme Density", "decade": "Decade"},
    height=430,
)
fig.update_layout(
    showlegend=False,
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=20, b=0),
)
fig.show()
```

Rhyme density remains relatively high and stable from the 1980s through the 2010s, with medians consistently around 0.65–0.75 and distributions concentrated in the upper half of the range. The 1980s show the tightest clustering near the top, while the 1990s and 2000s introduce more spread downward without meaningfully shifting the median. The 2010s maintain a similar central tendency but with a slightly longer lower tail. The most striking change comes in the 2020s, as  the median drops to around 0.4–0.5 and the interquartile range widens considerably.

## Language Distribution by Decade
```{python}
#| label: language-by-decade
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Detected language distribution by decade."

# bin rare languages into "other"
lang_df = master_df.dropna(subset=["language"]).copy()
top_langs = lang_df["language"].value_counts().head(5).index.tolist()
lang_df["language_grouped"] = lang_df["language"].apply(
    lambda x: x if x in top_langs else "other"
)

lang_counts = (
    lang_df
    .groupby(["decade", "language_grouped"])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="count")
)
# normalize to proportion within decade
lang_counts["proportion"] = lang_counts.groupby("decade")["count"].transform(
    lambda x: x / x.sum()
)

fig = px.bar(
    lang_counts,
    x="decade", y="proportion",
    color="language_grouped",
    category_orders={"decade": decade_order},
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Safe,
    labels={"proportion": "Proportion", "decade": "Decade", "language_grouped": "Language"},
    height=430,
    barmode="stack",
)
fig.update_layout(
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=20, b=0),
    yaxis_tickformat=".0%",
    legend_title="Language",
)
fig.show()
```

English dominates the corpus throughout, but its share erodes dramatically over time. From roughly 85% in the 1980s, it dips to around 73% in the 1990s and 2000s, recovers slightly in the 2010s, then collapses to just about 44% in 2020s. Spanish grew steadily from roughly 5% in the 1980s to nearly 30% by the 2020s, directly mirroring Latin music's mainstream rise. French maintains a small but consistent presence across all decades. The "other" category expands noticeably in the 2020s, likely capturing the rise of K-pop and other non-Western music. Turkish (tr) and Tagalog (tl) appear as minor but persistent contributors from the 1990s onward, reflecting the global diversity of popular music even in earlier decades.

## Top 10 Most Viewed Songs by Decade
```{python}
#| label: top-songs-pageviews
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Top 10 most-viewed songs on Genius per decade. Use the dropdown to browse each era."

buttons = []

        args=[{"visible": visibility}],

    height=420,
```
